explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says to charge the believers before God to avoid quarreling over words (2 Timothy 2:14). You know the kind. It starts over one little word and ends with somebody muting the group chat. Paul says to steer clear of it.

Money doesn't come up in this verse, friend. The fight Paul names is quarreling over words. He says to charge the believers before God to avoid it. Keep your eyes on the verse and the answer is sitting right there.
No land in this verse, baker. Nobody is out measuring property lines here. The fight Paul names is quarreling over words, and he wants the believers charged before God to avoid it.

Ruin, baker. Paul says quarreling over words succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin. Notice it's the listeners. It's like arguing over who dropped the tray while the cookies sit on the floor getting cold.

Wisdom would be a nice surprise, friend, but that's not what Paul says. He says quarreling over words succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin. Only. That means all that noise doesn't send anybody home with wisdom.
I wish it worked that way, baker. But quarreling over words doesn't bring people together. Paul says it succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin. Unity is not on the list.

The word of truth, baker. Paul wants Timothy to be an unashamed workman who accurately handles it. I handle my dough with care, and this is way more important than dough. A good workman respects what's in his hands.
Not this time, friend. Paul doesn't mention money in this verse. The workman he describes accurately handles the word of truth. That's the thing worth being careful with.
No records in this verse, baker. Paul doesn't bring up any paperwork here. The workman is the one who accurately handles the word of truth. Nobody is filing anything.
Spread, baker. Paul says the talk of such men will spread like gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17). It's a heavy picture, and he means it to be. Empty chatter doesn't stay in one spot.
I'd love for it to fade, friend. But Paul doesn't say that. He says the talk of such men will spread like gangrene. It moves outward, it doesn't wear away.

Healing is a lovely word, baker, but it's the opposite of the picture here. Paul says the talk of such men will spread like gangrene. Nothing about that sounds like getting better. He's warning Timothy, not comforting him.

True, baker. Paul says Hymenaeus and Philetus claim the resurrection has already occurred (2 Timothy 2:18). He names them and he names what they say. That's the teaching he says has deviated from the truth.

Close, but this one is true, friend. Paul says Hymenaeus and Philetus claim that the resurrection has already occurred (2 Timothy 2:18). That's exactly what the verse says they're teaching. It's right there in black and white.
Undermining their faith, baker. Paul says they undermine the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:18). Think of pulling out the bottom cookie from a tall stack. Everything above it starts to wobble.

explanations.answer: Pulling them back to the law
explanations.explanation: The law doesn't come up in this verse, friend. Paul says Hymenaeus and Philetus undermine the faith of some. That's what their teaching is doing to those believers.
Nope, baker, nobody is getting sent out here. Paul says they undermine the faith of some. It's the faith itself that's under attack, not anybody's travel plans.

explanations.answer: The Lord knows those who are His
explanations.explanation: The Lord knows those who are His, baker. That's the first saying on the seal (2 Timothy 2:19). Some people's faith may be shaking, but the foundation stands. He knows His own.

explanations.answer: Every teacher must be tested first
explanations.explanation: That one isn't on the seal, friend. The first saying is “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Timothy 2:19). Paul doesn't put a testing rule on it. It's a comfort, not a checklist.

explanations.answer: Hold fast to the old traditions
explanations.explanation: Not on the seal, baker. The first saying is “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Timothy 2:19). Traditions aren't mentioned in that verse. The seal is about the Lord knowing His own.

Iniquity, baker. The seal says, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.” (2 Timothy 2:19) Calling on the Lord comes with turning away. Both halves of that seal belong together.
Fear is a good guess, friend, but it's not in the seal. The seal says, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.” (2 Timothy 2:19) That's the word Paul uses.

Wealth doesn't show up in this verse, baker. The seal says, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.” (2 Timothy 2:19) Iniquity is the thing to turn from. My bank account was never the issue anyway.

True, baker. Paul says some vessels are for honorable use, but others are for common use (2 Timothy 2:20). Every house needs both kinds. Even a kitchen has the nice platter and the everyday mixing bowl.

This one is true, friend. Paul says some vessels are for honorable use, but others are for common use (2 Timothy 2:20). So the large house in his picture has both. Common use is right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: Cleansing himself of what is unfit
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor (2 Timothy 2:21). It's about being cleansed, not about being fancy. Anybody can be that kind of vessel.

Hard work is a fine thing, friend, but Paul doesn't say that here. He says it's the one who cleanses himself of what is unfit who will be a vessel for honor. There's no race against the other vessels in this verse.
No guest list in this verse, baker. Paul says the one who cleanses himself of what is unfit will be a vessel for honor. It's about the vessel being cleansed, not who gets served.

Prepared for every good work, baker. Paul says the vessel for honor is sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work (2 Timothy 2:21). That's an apron-on, oven-hot kind of readiness. Ready for whatever good work comes in.
That sounds comforting, friend, but Paul doesn't say it. He says the vessel for honor is sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work. Prepared is the word, not protected.
Paul doesn't set up a ranking, baker. He says the vessel for honor is sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work. Nobody is being crowned above the rest.

explanations.answer: Others who call on the Lord from a pure heart
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says to pursue these things together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. Timothy isn't meant to chase them alone. It's better with company, like a batch that goes faster with extra hands.

explanations.answer: Others who have suffered hardship for the Lord
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend, but that's not what this verse says. Paul says to pursue these things together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. That's the company he points to.

explanations.answer: Others who have studied the Scriptures since childhood
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse, baker. Paul says to pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. A pure heart is what he names, not a long study record.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the opposite: a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing (2 Timothy 2:24). Nothing in the verse carves out an exception. The servant stays kind even when the truth is at stake.

False, baker. Paul says a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing (2 Timothy 2:24). That's the whole job description. I'd put that on my own bakery wall.
Kind, baker. Paul says a servant of the Lord must be kind to everyone. Everyone, not just the people who agree with him. That's a wide circle.
Teach, baker. Paul says the servant must be able to teach. That's a skill, and it goes right alongside the kindness. Showing somebody how, without making them feel small.
Harsh is the opposite of what Paul says, friend. The servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone. Kind is the word on the page.
Leading is a fine thing, baker, but it's not what Paul says here. He says the servant must be able to teach. Teaching is the skill he names.
Judging isn't on Paul's list, friend. He says the servant must be kind to everyone and able to teach. Those are the two words that fit the blanks.
Gently, baker. Paul says the servant must gently reprove those who oppose him. How you say it matters as much as what you say. Think of pressing a cookie stamp. Too hard and you crack the dough.
Paul doesn't say publicly, friend. He says the servant must gently reprove those who oppose him. Gentleness is the word he picks, and he leaves the audience out.
Speed isn't what Paul asks for, baker. He says the servant must gently reprove those who oppose him. Gently is the word, no stopwatch required.
Repentance, baker. Paul says to reprove in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth. Notice who grants it. The hope is that God may grant it.
Success sounds good, friend, but it's not what Paul says. He says the hope is that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth. The goal is repentance, not a win.
Rest is a nice thing, baker, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says the hope is that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth. Repentance is what fits the blank.

The snare of the devil, baker. Paul says they will come to their senses and escape it, since the devil has taken them captive to his will (2 Timothy 2:26). A snare is a trap, and they get out of it. That's good news, and it starts with God granting repentance.
Rome isn't mentioned in this verse, friend. Paul says they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil. That's the trap in view here.
No famine in this passage, baker. Paul says they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil. That's the thing they get free from.
